user_input: How many total CT brain scans were included in the dataset for the ResNet-18 stroke study, how many were allocated to training, and what were the three diagnostic categories?
reference: The dataset comprised 6653 CT brain scans in total, with 4655 scans allocated to the training set (70% split), categorized into three diagnostic categories: normal, ischemic stroke (ischemia), and hemorrhagic stroke (bleeding).
reference_contexts:
In this paper, a ResNet-18 model was trained on 6653 CT brain scans (hemorrhagic stroke, ischemia, normal) with two-phase fine-tuning and transfer learning, XRAI
explainability analysis, and web-based clinical decision support system integration.

Each CT scan slice in the dataset is labeled with one of three diagnostic categories: normal (indicating no evidence of stroke), ischemic stroke, or hemorrhagic stroke due to intracranial bleeding. Among the 6653 images, 4428 are labeled as normal, 1131 as ischemic stroke, and 1094 as hemorrhagic stroke... The training set comprised 765 cases of hemorrhagic stroke, 791 ischemic cases, and 3099 normal cases.

user_input: In the study A Hybrid Deep Learning Approach for Improved Detection and Prediction of Brain Stroke by Thakre et al., what percentage of all strokes worldwide are ischemic strokes and what percentage are hemorrhagic strokes?
reference: Ischemic strokes make up almost 87% of all strokes worldwide, while hemorrhagic strokes are liable for 10–15% of stroke cases around the world.
reference_contexts: There are two essential kinds of strokes: ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes [1]. Ischemic strokes, which make up almost 87% of all strokes worldwide, happen when a blood coagulation or blockage keeps blood from arriving at the mind, denying it of oxygen and nutrients [1]. Hemorrhagic strokes, liable for 10–15% of stroke cases around the world, happen when a vein in the cerebrum breaks, causing draining and pressure that harms mind cells [1].

user_input: What primary challenge occurs in brain CT image classification when utilizing machine learning and deep learning algorithms for minority stroke lesions in the StyleGAN study?
reference: Brain computed tomography image classification frequently suffers from a class imbalance problem, making it difficult to effectively extract deep-detailed features from instances of minority stroke lesions.
reference_contexts: However, brain computed tomography image classification using machine learning and deep learning algorithms frequently suffers from a class imbalance problem, making it difficult to effectively extract deep-detailed features from instances of minority stroke lesions.

However, in actual medical applications, stroke examples are significantly fewer than normal samples, leading to an imbalance in class distribution. This causes traditional classification models to lean towards normal examples during training, thereby negatively affecting stroke detection accuracy.
